This won't be popular, but no. Not in the sense that the government should have to provide it. But I think uninhibited access to it (e.g. net-neutrality) is a necessity. People who want it should be able to get it.

I say this because there are MANY people who live just fine without it. A necessity is something you need (sorry to be circular there). But you don't need the Internet. You do need water or you'll die of thirst and heat or you'll freeze to death. Electricity is also a bit tenuous, but in a more modern world so very much of what we do depends on having power.

But Internet? My octogenarian mother lives without Internet just fine. She's never had it and doesn't want it. Many many people live just fine without access to it, and have been doing so for tens of thousands of years.

But I would concede that in our modern society, access to Internet is critical. And even more critical that when you have access, it's not being filtered or censored, as in many parts of the world.

Generally speaking I believe that it has become the physical manifestation of a number of fundamental human rights - education, free speech and opinion, association etc.

Technically and specifically :

I believe that the Internet (i.e. the physical network infrastructure allowing communications) is not a fundamental neccessity any more or less than other physical infrastructures delivering services such as electricity and water. We don't say the water pipe is a neccessity, we say access to clean drinking water is.

On the other side of the coin, the World Wide Web ( which as TYL, is a distinctly different thing) I believe, a necessity and cannot be and should not be restricted or controlled by governments other than as the custodians of a service delivered for the public good. TBL did not patent the WWW for a reason - Because he forsaw that it had the potential to become exactly that - knowledge becoming as fundamental to life as water - a human right.

As far as the FCC decision goes /shrug The US is not the world. Get over yourselves. The FCC decision won't change things in China or in oppressive regimes. Show me an FCC regulation stopping virtual colonialism by Facebook et. al. in Africa for instance, and I'll take notice.
